        function speakText(text, rate=.55){
            if(!text) return;
            if(!("speechSynthesis" in window) || !("SpeechSynthesisUtterance" in window)){
                alert("المتصفح الحالي لا يدعم تحويل النص إلى صوت. جرّب Chrome أو Edge.");
                return;
            }
            const synth=window.speechSynthesis;
            synth.cancel();
            const speakNow=()=>{
                try{
                    const u=new SpeechSynthesisUtterance(String(text));
                    u.lang="en-US";
                    u.rate=Math.max(.25,Math.min(1.2,Number(rate)||.55));
                    u.pitch=1;
                    u.volume=1;
                    const voices=synth.getVoices();
                    const voice=voices.find(v=>/^en-US$/i.test(v.lang)) || voices.find(v=>/^en/i.test(v.lang));
                    if(voice) u.voice=voice;
                    synth.speak(u);
                }catch(e){ console.error("TTS error:",e); }
            };
            const voices=synth.getVoices();
            if(voices.length){ speakNow(); }
            else {
                speakNow();
                setTimeout(()=>{ if(!synth.speaking) speakNow(); },120);
            }
        }

        window.addEventListener("beforeunload", () => {
            if ("speechSynthesis" in window) window.speechSynthesis.cancel();
        });

            const stableHash=(value)=>{let h=2166136261;for(let i=0;i<String(value).length;i++){h^=String(value).charCodeAt(i);h=Math.imul(h,16777619);}return h>>>0;};
            const stableShuffle=(arr,seed)=>{const a=[...arr];let x=stableHash(seed)||1;for(let i=a.length-1;i>0;i--){x^=x<<13;x^=x>>>17;x^=x<<5;const j=Math.abs(x)% (i+1);[a[i],a[j]]=[a[j],a[i]];}return a;};
            const enrichComprehensionQuestions=(source,type)=>{

                const answerKey=q=>`${key}|${q.id||q.q}`;
                const normalizeAnswer=v=>{
                let s=String(v??"").trim().toLowerCase();
                s=s.replace(/[’‘]/g,"'");
                const contractions={"doesn't":"does not","don't":"do not","didn't":"did not","isn't":"is not","aren't":"are not","wasn't":"was not","weren't":"were not","can't":"cannot","couldn't":"could not","won't":"will not","wouldn't":"would not","shouldn't":"should not","mustn't":"must not","haven't":"have not","hasn't":"has not","hadn't":"had not"};
                Object.keys(contractions).forEach(k=>{s=s.replace(new RegExp('\\b'+k.replace(/[.*+?^${}()|[\]\\]/g,'\\$&')+'\\b','g'),contractions[k]);});
                // Punctuation is not a grammar-answer discriminator for these exercises.
                // Commas, hyphens, slashes, apostrophes, etc. become simple spaces.
                s=s.replace(/[^a-z0-9]+/g," ");
                return s.replace(/\s+/g," ").trim();
            };
                const getCorrectText=q=>q.correctText??q.answer??q.solution??(q.type==="mcq"?q.options?.[q.correct]:q.correct);

                    const a=quizAnswers[answerKey(q)];
                    if(q.type==="order") return Array.isArray(a)&&((q.firstOnly&&a.length>=1)||(!q.firstOnly&&a.length===q.words.length));
                    if(q.type==="match") return Array.isArray(a)&&a.length===q.pairs.length;
                    return a!==undefined&&a!=="";
                };
                const checkOne=(q,a)=>{
                    if(q.type==="mcq"||!q.type) return a===q.correct;
                    if(q.type==="truefalse") return a===q.correct;
                    if(["fill","correct","transform","conjugate"].includes(q.type)){
                        const accepted=[q.answer,q.correctText,...(q.accepted||[])].filter(x=>x!==undefined).map(normalizeAnswer);
                        return accepted.includes(normalizeAnswer(a));
                    }
                    if(q.type==="order") return Array.isArray(a)&&((q.firstOnly ? a[0]?.split("|")[0]===q.correctOrder[0] : a.map(x=>x.split("|")[0]).join(" ")===q.correctOrder.join(" ")));
                    if(q.type==="match") return Array.isArray(a)&&q.pairs.every((pair,i)=>a[i]===pair[1]);
                    return false;
                };
                const verify=()=>{
                    if(!questions.every(isAnswered)){setFeedback("⚠️ أكمل كل الأسئلة أولًا.");return;}
                    const wrongIndexes=[];
                    questions.forEach((q,i)=>{
                        const a=quizAnswers[answerKey(q)];
                        if(!checkOne(q,a)) wrongIndexes.push(i+1);
                    });
                    if(wrongIndexes.length===0){

                        onSuccess&&onSuccess();

                    }
                    const nextAttempt=attempt+1;
                    setQuizAttempts(p=>({...p,[key]:nextAttempt}));
                    if(nextAttempt>=3){
                        setQuizSolutions(p=>({...p,[key]:true}));
                        setFeedback(`❌ هذه هي المحاولة الثالثة. الإجابات الصحيحة ظهرت أسفل الأسئلة. أعد الدرس من البداية.`);
                        setTimeout(()=>window.scrollTo({top:0,behavior:"smooth"}),80);
                    }else{
                        setFeedback(`❌ توجد أخطاء في الأسئلة: ${wrongIndexes.join("، ")}. المحاولة ${nextAttempt} من 3. عدّل إجاباتك وحاول مرة أخرى.`);
                    }
                };
                const renderOne=(q)=>{
                    const a=quizAnswers[answerKey(q)];
                    if((q.type||"mcq")==="mcq") {
                        const opts=q.options.map((text,index)=>({text,index}));
                        const shuffled=stableShuffle(opts,`${activeLesson?.id||"lesson"}:${q.id||q.q}`);
                        return <div className="choice-grid" dir={type==="grammar"?"ltr":"rtl"}>{shuffled.map((o,i)=><div key={o.index} className={`choice ${a===o.index?"selected":""}`} dir={type==="grammar"?"ltr":"rtl"} onClick={()=>setQuizAnswers(p=>({...p,[answerKey(q)]:o.index}))}>{o.text}{a===o.index?" ✓":""}</div>)}</div>;
                    }

            const makeGrammarMcq=(questions)=>{
                const source=Array.isArray(questions)?questions:[];
                return source.map((q,i)=>{
                    if((q.type||"mcq")==="mcq") return {...q,type:"mcq"};
                    const correct=String(q.answer??q.correctText??q.solution??q.correct??"").trim();
                    let distractors=[];
                    if(correct){
                        if(q.type==="fill"||q.type==="conjugate"){
                            distractors=[correct.replace(/s$/i,""),`does ${correct}`,`is ${correct}`];
                            if(correct.includes(" / ")) distractors=[correct.split(" / ").reverse().join(" / "),correct.replace(" / "," "),`do / ${correct.split(" / ").pop()}`];
                        } else {
                            const original=String(q.q||"").replace(/^(Correct|Change|Make|Ask|Complete|صحح|حوّل|أكمل).*?:\s*/i,"").trim();
                            distractors=[original,`The sentence needs a different verb form.`,`None of these.`];
                        }
                    } else distractors=["Not stated in the lesson.","The opposite form.","None of these."];
                    const opts=stableShuffle([correct,...distractors.filter(x=>x&&x!==correct).slice(0,3)],`${activeLesson?.id||"g"}:${q.id||i}`);
                    return {...q,type:"mcq",options:opts,correct:Math.max(0,opts.indexOf(correct)),correctText:correct};
                });
            };

            const renderGrammar=()=>{
                const d=activeLesson||demoData.grammar;
                const pages=grammarLessonPages[activeLesson?.id] || [];
                const page=pages[Math.min(grammarPageIndex,pages.length-1)] || pages[0];
                const last=pages.length>0 && grammarPageIndex===pages.length-1;
                if(!pages.length) return <div className="study-box"><h3>{d.title}</h3><div className="notice-box">لم تتم إضافة صفحات الشرح لهذا الدرس بعد.</div></div>;
                if(grammarQuizUnlocked) return renderQuestions(makeGrammarMcq(getGrammarQuiz(d)),"grammar");
                return <div className="grammar-reader-overlay">
                    <div className="grammar-reader" role="dialog" aria-modal="true">
                        <div className="grammar-reader-head">
                            <div className="grammar-reader-brand"><div className="grammar-reader-brand-icon">G</div><div><div className="grammar-reader-title">{d.title}</div><div className="grammar-reader-subtitle">Grammar Lesson Reader · Interactive Pages</div></div></div>
                            <button type="button" className="grammar-reader-close" onClick={()=>{setActiveLesson(null);setGrammarPageIndex(0)}}>✕ إغلاق الدرس</button>
                        </div>
                        <div className="grammar-reader-progress"><div className="grammar-reader-progress-fill" style={{width:`${((grammarPageIndex+1)/pages.length)*100}%`}}/></div>
                        <div className="grammar-reader-body" ref={grammarReaderBodyRef}>
                            <article className="grammar-reader-page">
                                <div className="grammar-page-kicker">Grammar · Page {grammarPageIndex+1}</div>
                                <h1 className="grammar-page-title">{page.title}</h1>
                                <div className="grammar-page-content" dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{__html:page.html}}/>
                                <div className="grammar-page-footer"><span>GenPrime English · B1</span><span>صفحة {grammarPageIndex+1} من {pages.length}</span></div>
                            </article>
                        </div>
                        <div className="grammar-reader-nav">

Profile: The Revitalization of Industrial City Districts","passage":"For much of the twentieth century, industrial districts were important centers of economic activity. Factories, warehouses, workshops, and transport facilities provided jobs for thousands of people. As industries changed and many factories closed, however, some of these neighborhoods became empty and neglected.\n\nIn recent years, a number of cities have started to revitalize former industrial areas. Instead of destroying old buildings completely, city planners are finding new uses for them. Old factories may become offices, restaurants, art galleries, cultural centers, or apartment buildings.\n\nOne example can be found in the Riverside district. The area was once home to several large factories, but most of them closed more than twenty years ago. For a long time, the neighborhood had few businesses and attracted little investment.\n\nThe city eventually began a redevelopment project. The first stage focused on improving public spaces. Streets were repaired, lighting was improved, and an old railway path was transformed into a walking and cycling route. Small parks were also created between existing buildings.\n\nThe second stage encouraged businesses to move into the area. The city offered financial support to companies willing to renovate old industrial buildings. As a result, several technology companies, cafés, design studios, and small businesses opened there.\n\nThe changes also affected the local community. New jobs became available, and the area became more attractive to visitors. Some residents were pleased with the improvements because the neighborhood felt safer and more active.\n\nHowever, revitalization can create problems as well. When an area becomes more popular, property prices and rents may increase. This can make it difficult for some long-term residents to continue living there. Small businesses may also face higher costs.\n\nFor this reason, successful redevelopment requires more than new buildings and attractive streets. City governments need to consider the people who already live in the neighborhood. few years ago, watching television usually meant waiting for a particular program to start at a particular time. Today, people may watch different shows at different speeds. This can make conversations about television more complicated because friends may be at different points in the same series.\n\nAnother issue is the effect of constant entertainment on attention. When viewers become used to moving immediately from one episode to another, they may find it difficult to stop. Streaming companies understand this behavior and often design their platforms to encourage continued viewing.\n\nHowever, binge-watching is not necessarily harmful. Unlike traditional gasoline-powered cars, electric vehicles do not burn fuel inside an engine, so there is no exhaust pipe releasing carbon dioxide and other pollutants directly into the air.\n\nThis difference can make electric cars appear to be completely clean. However, the reality is more complicated. To understand their environmental impact, it is necessary to look beyond what happens when the car is being driven.\n\nOne important factor is electricity production. Electric cars need to be charged, and the environmental benefit of charging depends partly on how that electricity is generated. If a country produces most of its electricity from renewable sources such as solar, wind, or hydropower, charging an electric car can have a relatively low carbon footprint. If electricity mainly comes from coal or other fossil fuels, the overall emissions are higher.\n\nAnother issue is the production of the vehicle itself, especially its battery. Electric-car batteries require materials such as lithium, nickel, and other minerals. Mining and processing these materials can require significant amounts of energy and water. In some regions, mining can also create environmental and social problems if it is not properly managed.\n\nThis does not necessarily mean that electric cars are worse for the environment than gasoline cars. Instead, it means that the comparison should consider the vehicle's entire life cycle. Its reddish surface, enormous valleys, and ancient landscapes suggest that the planet was once very different from the cold and dry world we see today. One of the biggest questions in Mars research is whether liquid water ever existed there in large amounts and, if so, whether it could have created conditions suitable for life.\n\nScientists have strong evidence that water once existed on the surface of Mars. Spacecraft and robotic missions have found geological features that appear to have been shaped by flowing water. Scientists have also identified minerals that normally form when rocks interact with water. These discoveries suggest that ancient Mars was not always dry.\n\nThe important question is what happened to that water. Mars has a much thinner atmosphere than Earth, which makes it difficult for liquid water to remain stable on the surface for long periods. Over time, much of the planet's surface water may have disappeared into space as the atmosphere became thinner. Some water may also have become frozen underground or trapped inside minerals.\n\nToday, scientists continue to search for evidence of underground water. Radar instruments on spacecraft can send signals beneath the surface and detect differences between layers of rock and ice. In some areas, researchers have found signs that could be connected to large amounts of underground ice. However, interpreting these signals is difficult, and scientists must consider other possible explanations.\n\nThe search for water is not simply about finding a useful resource for future astronauts. Water is one of the most important ingredients for life as we know it. On Earth, wherever there is liquid water and a suitable environment, some form of life can often survive. Therefore, finding evidence of ancient or present water on Mars could help scientists understand whether the planet was ever capable of supporting life.\n\nHowever, scientists are careful not to confuse water with evidence of life. The presence of water does not automatically mean that living organisms existed. Scientists would need additional evidence, such as chemical signs or structures that could reasonably be connected to biological activity.\n\nFuture missions may help answer some of these questions. Robots can collect and analyze rocks, study the atmosphere, and examine locations that may contain water or signs of ancient environments. Scientists are particularly interested in areas where water may have remained protected from the harsh conditions on the surface.\n\nThe search for water on Mars is therefore a search for more than a substance. It is a way of reconstructing the planet's history. By understanding where water existed, how long it remained, and what happened to it, scientists can build a clearer picture of Mars as it once was.\n\nFor now, we know that Mars had water in its distant past, but many details remain uncertain. We do not yet know exactly how much water existed, how long it remained on the surface, or whether Mars ever supported life. Producing more energy from local renewable sources can reduce some of these risks.\n\nHowever, reaching ambitious targets will not be easy. Renewable energy has expanded rapidly in many parts of the world, but energy systems were traditionally designed around large power stations using fossil fuels. Moving toward renewable sources requires changes to electricity networks, storage systems, transportation, and industrial infrastructure.\n\nOne of the biggest challenges is that some renewable sources are dependent on natural conditions. Solar panels produce less electricity at night or during periods of heavy cloud, while wind turbines depend on wind conditions. This does not mean renewable energy is unreliable, but it does mean that electricity systems need ways to manage changes in production.\n\nEnergy storage can help solve part of this problem. Batteries, for example, can store electricity when production is high and release it when demand increases. Other technologies are also being developed. However, storage remains expensive in some situations, and large-scale systems require significant investment.\n\nAnother challenge is the difference between countries. A country with large areas of sunlight may have excellent opportunities for solar power, while another country may have stronger winds or greater access to water. Financial resources, geography, existing infrastructure, and government policies all influence how quickly renewable energy can grow.\n\nThere is also a social dimension to the transition. New energy projects can create jobs and investment, but they may also cause disagreements. Local communities sometimes oppose large wind farms, solar projects, or transmission lines because they are concerned about land use, appearance, environmental effects, or changes to their neighborhoods.\n\nDespite these difficulties, supporters argue that the transition could bring long-term benefits. Renewable energy can reduce emissions, create new industries, and make countries less dependent on imported fuels. It may also encourage technological innovation as companies compete to develop cheaper and more efficient systems.\n\nExperts generally agree that setting a target is easier than achieving it. Governments must create clear policies, invest in infrastructure, train workers, and cooperate with businesses and local communities. A target without practical planning may remain only a number on paper.\n\nThe 2030 renewable energy goals therefore represent both an opportunity and a test. The world already has many of the technologies needed for a cleaner energy system, but the difficult part is expanding them at the necessary scale. Telemedicine has changed this experience by allowing patients to communicate with healthcare professionals through video calls, phone calls, or online platforms. What was once a limited service has become a practical option for many people.\n\nOne major advantage of telemedicine is convenience. A patient may be able to speak with a doctor without taking time off work or travelling a long distance. This can be particularly useful for people who live far from medical centers or have difficulty travelling. It can also reduce the number of people visiting hospitals for minor problems.\n\nTelemedicine can be useful for follow-up appointments as well. For example, a doctor may not need to examine a patient physically if the purpose of the appointment is simply to discuss test results or check whether a treatment is working. A patient living in a small town may have difficulty finding a specialist locally. Online consultations can sometimes connect that patient with a professional in another city or region.\n\nHowever, telemedicine has clear limitations. Some medical conditions require a physical examination. A doctor may need to listen to a patient's heart, examine an injury, measure certain physical signs, or perform a procedure. A video call cannot provide all of these possibilities.\n\nTechnology itself can also create problems. A weak internet connection, poor camera quality, or unfamiliar software may interrupt an appointment. Older patients or people with limited digital skills may find online healthcare difficult to use. In addition, not everyone has reliable internet access or a suitable private space for a medical conversation.\n\nPrivacy is another important concern. Medical information is highly sensitive, so healthcare providers must protect patient data. Patients also need to understand how their information is collected, stored, and shared. Convenience should not come at the cost of security.\n\nThere is also a question about the quality of communication. Doctors often learn important information by observing a patient's behavior, appearance, or physical condition. During a virtual appointment, some of these details may be harder to notice. Patients may also find it easier to explain certain problems in person.\n\nFor these reasons, telemedicine is unlikely to completely replace traditional medical care. Instead, the two systems can support each other. Virtual appointments may be appropriate for simple consultations, follow-ups, and some routine problems, while face-to-face care remains essential for situations that require physical examination or immediate treatment.\n\nThe future of telemedicine may therefore depend less on choosing between online and traditional healthcare and more on knowing when each method is appropriate. audiences. A successful television campaign could make a brand familiar to millions of people. Today, however, businesses have another option: working with social media influencers, particularly micro-influencers with relatively small but highly engaged audiences.\n\nA micro-influencer usually has a smaller following than a celebrity or major online creator. The exact number can vary, but the important difference is not simply the size of the audience. Micro-influencers often focus on a specific subject, such as fitness, technology, cooking, fashion, travel, or education. Their followers may share a strong interest in that particular area.\n\nThis specialization can be valuable to businesses. A company selling professional fitness equipment, for example, does not necessarily need its advertisement to reach millions of random television viewers. It may prefer to reach a smaller group of people who are already interested in exercise. A micro-influencer can provide access to this more focused audience.\n\nAnother reason companies work with micro-influencers is trust. Followers often feel that smaller creators are more approachable and relatable than celebrities. When an influencer regularly shares personal experiences and responds to comments, followers may develop a stronger relationship with the creator. As a result, a recommendation may feel more like advice from someone familiar rather than a traditional advertisement.\n\nHowever, influencer marketing is not automatically successful. A large number of followers does not guarantee that people will buy a product. Some accounts may have inactive followers, and others may attract attention without influencing purchasing decisions.\n\nBusinesses therefore need to examine more than follower counts. They may look at engagement, audience characteristics, previous campaigns, and the quality of the creator's content. A smaller creator with a highly active audience can sometimes produce better results than a much larger account.\n\nThere are also risks. If an influencer behaves irresponsibly or becomes involved in a public controversy, the associated brand may suffer damage to its reputation. Companies must therefore choose partners carefully and make sure that the influencer's values and behavior are compatible with the brand.\n\nTransparency is another important issue. In many markets, influencers are expected to clearly indicate when they have been paid or given products to promote. If followers believe that a recommendation is completely independent when it is actually sponsored, they may feel misled.\n\nDespite these challenges, the growth of micro-influencer marketing reflects a broader change in advertising. Consumers are increasingly exposed to personalized content rather than a single message designed for everyone. Instead of asking, “How many people can we reach?”, marketers may increasingly ask, “Which people do we want to reach, and how can we communicate with them effectively?”\n\nTelevision advertising is unlikely to disappear completely. Large brands may still use television when they want broad public awareness. But for companies with specialized products or limited advertising budgets, micro-influencers can provide a more targeted alternative.\n\nThe most effective strategy may not be choosing one method over another. A company could use television to create general awareness while using influencers to build trust within specific communities. In this sense, micro-influencers are not simply replacing traditional advertising; they are changing how businesses think about the relationship between audience size, trust, and marketing New styles appear in stores and online shops almost constantly, encouraging people to replace their clothes more frequently. While this system offers affordable choices, its true cost may be paid by workers and communities far from the consumers who buy the products.\n\nA large part of the global clothing industry depends on factories in developing countries. These factories can provide millions of jobs and contribute to economic growth. For some workers, employment in garment production may offer a more stable income than other available forms of work. Therefore, it would be too simple to describe the entire industry as harmful.\n\nThe problem is that low prices create strong pressure throughout the supply chain. International brands compete to sell clothing cheaply, and factories compete to receive contracts. When buyers demand lower prices and faster production, factory owners may try to reduce labor costs or increase working hours. In poorly regulated environments, workers can become especially vulnerable.\n\nWorking conditions are therefore an important part of the debate. Low wages, long working hours, unsafe buildings, and limited worker protection have been reported in parts of the industry. Not every factory has the same conditions, but the existence of serious problems shows why cheap clothing should not be judged only by its price in a store.\n\nEnvironmental damage adds another layer to the issue. Producing clothing requires water, energy, chemicals, and raw materials. Large quantities of unwanted clothing are eventually thrown away, creating additional waste. When consumers purchase items they only wear a few times, the environmental cost of production becomes harder to justify.\n\nSupporters of fast fashion argue that affordable clothing allows people with limited incomes to participate in modern fashion. They also point out that the industry creates employment and supports businesses in countries where manufacturing is an important part of the economy.\n\nCritics do not necessarily argue that clothing production should disappear. Instead, they question the speed and scale of the current system. They believe companies should improve working conditions, reduce waste, use resources more responsibly, and provide clearer information about where products are made.\n\nConsumers also have a role. Buying fewer but better-quality items can reduce unnecessary consumption. Repairing clothes instead of immediately replacing them can extend their useful life. Consumers can also pay attention to company policies and choose businesses that demonstrate stronger environmental and labor standards.\n\nHowever, placing all responsibility on consumers would be unfair. A person with a limited budget may not be able to choose the most expensive ethical products. Governments and companies have greater power to establish minimum standards and change production systems.\n\nThe issue is therefore more complicated than deciding whether fast fashion is simply good or bad. It involves employment, poverty, consumer choice, business competition, workers' rights, and environmental protection. Any serious solution must consider all of these factors.\n\nIn my view, the central problem is not that people want affordable clothes. The problem is a system that encourages extremely rapid production and consumption while hiding many of its social and environmental costs. Smart Cities: Surveillance Concerns","passage":"Cities around the world are becoming “smarter.” Traffic lights can change automatically when roads become crowded, public transport systems can collect information about passengers, and cameras can help authorities identify unusual activity in busy areas. These technologies are often presented as practical solutions to modern urban problems. However, as cities collect more information about the people who live in them, an important question appears: how much surveillance is too much?\n\nA smart city depends on data. Sensors may record traffic levels, air quality, energy consumption, or the movement of vehicles. Some systems can also collect information about people, either directly or indirectly. For example, a camera in a train station may be designed to improve security, but the same camera can potentially track where people go and when they arrive. When many systems are connected, individual pieces of information can create a much more detailed picture of a person's daily life.\n\nSupporters of smart-city technology argue that this information can make cities safer and more efficient. If authorities know where traffic problems usually occur, they can adjust traffic lights or improve roads. If public transport data shows that a particular station becomes overcrowded every morning, officials can increase the number of buses or trains. In emergencies, connected cameras and communication systems may help emergency services respond more quickly.\n\nThe problem is that efficiency and privacy do not always point in the same direction. A system may work extremely well while still creating risks for personal privacy. People may not know what information is being collected, how long it is stored, who can access it, or whether it can be used for a different purpose later.\n\nThis becomes especially complicated when private companies operate parts of a city's digital infrastructure. A technology company might provide cameras, software, or data-analysis systems. The company may have access to large amounts of information, even though citizens did not directly choose to share that information with the company. This raises questions about responsibility. If a system is misused, who should be held accountable: the government, the company, or both?\n\nAnother concern is that surveillance systems can affect behavior even when no one is actively watching. People may behave differently if they believe that their movements are constantly being recorded. A person might avoid attending a protest, visiting a particular location, or meeting certain people because they are worried about being monitored. In this way, surveillance can influence freedom without directly preventing anyone from doing anything.\n\nThere is also the issue of unequal impact. Technology does not automatically produce fairness. If surveillance tools are used more heavily in certain neighborhoods, the people living there may experience greater monitoring than residents in other parts of the city. Similarly, if an automated system makes inaccurate assumptions about particular groups, those groups may face unnecessary attention or suspicion.\n\nNone of this means that smart-city technology should be rejected completely. The benefits can be significant, particularly when technology is used to solve genuine public problems. The real challenge is creating clear limits. Cities need transparent rules about what data can be collected, why it is collected, how long it can be kept, and who can use it.\n\nCitizens should also have a voice in these decisions. Smart-city projects are often introduced as technical improvements, but they can affect basic questions about privacy, freedom, and trust. These are not purely technical issues. They are social and political decisions as well.\n\nA truly smart city, therefore, should not simply be a city that collects more data. It should be a city that understands when data is useful and when collecting it becomes unnecessary or harmful. Technology can make urban life more convenient, but trust is also part of a city's infrastructure. Without it, even the most advanced system may fail to serve the people it was designed to help.","questions":[{"id":"r28-q1","type":"fill","q":"What is the main purpose of the article?","answer":"To I expected the trip to be exciting, but I underestimated how much living abroad would change my understanding of ordinary things.\n\nMy first destination was southern Europe. I rented a small apartment in a quiet neighborhood and immediately noticed that daily life moved at a different pace. People often stopped at cafés without appearing to be in a hurry. Shops closed for several hours during the afternoon, and dinner usually began much later than I was used to. At first, these habits were inconvenient. After a few weeks, however, I began to appreciate them. I realized that my idea of being productive had been strongly connected to speed.\n\nEurope was also where I learned that traveling and living somewhere are not the same experience. As a tourist, I had always focused on famous buildings, museums, and restaurants. As a temporary resident, I became interested in supermarkets, bus routes, laundry services, and neighborhood conversations. These ordinary details gave me a much clearer picture of local life.\n\nAfter several months, I moved to East Africa. The change was much greater than I had expected. The language, climate, transportation, and social habits were different. My first few weeks were difficult because many things I normally did automatically required conscious effort. I had to ask questions more often, pay closer attention, and accept that my usual solutions would not always work.\n\nOne afternoon, my internet connection suddenly stopped during an important online meeting. In my previous apartment, I would have restarted the router and continued working. Here, the situation required a different approach. I walked to a nearby café, explained the problem, and finished the meeting from there. It was a small event, but it taught me something important: independence is not the same as doing everything alone. Sometimes independence means knowing how to find help quickly.\n\nLiving in East Africa also challenged some of my assumptions. Before arriving, I had imagined that I would spend most of my free time exploring. Instead, I often preferred sitting with local people, listening to conversations, and learning how the community worked. I became less interested in collecting experiences and more interested in understanding them.\n\nMy final destination was Southeast Asia. By this point, I had become much more comfortable with uncertainty. I could arrive in a new city without knowing exactly how the next week would look. I learned to compare prices, ask for directions, adapt my working hours, and solve small problems without becoming frustrated.\n\nHowever, the freedom also had a cost. Constant movement became tiring. Maintaining friendships across different time zones was difficult, and I sometimes missed having a familiar place to return to. I had imagined that flexibility would automatically make me happier. Instead, I discovered that flexibility is useful only when it is balanced with stability.\n\nOne of the most valuable lessons came from language. In each country, I spoke with people who had different accents and communication styles. Sometimes I understood every word but still missed the meaning because of cultural differences. At other times, my vocabulary was limited, but a gesture or facial expression helped me understand the situation. Communication, I realized, depends on much more than grammar.\n\nAt the end of the year, I returned home with fewer photographs than I had expected and far more notes than I had planned to write. The journey had not simply shown me three continents. It had changed the way I looked at routine, independence, communication, and comfort.\n\nI still enjoy traveling, but I no longer believe that the value of travel comes from the number of places visited. A person can cross ten borders without learning much. Another person can spend six months in one neighborhood and return with a completely different understanding of the world.\n\nThe biggest surprise was that I had started the year hoping to discover new countries. In many industries, employers expected applicants to have completed formal education before they would even consider them for a position. Technology, however, has complicated this traditional model. Today, a person may learn programming, cybersecurity, data analysis, or web development through university, but they can also develop many of the same skills through online courses, professional certificates, independent projects, and practical experience.\n\nThis change has created an important debate: if technology companies can evaluate what a person can actually do, rather than simply checking their educational background, is a university degree still necessary?\n\nThere are strong arguments on both sides. A university education can provide a structured learning environment. Students normally follow a planned curriculum, complete assignments, receive feedback, and study subjects that they might not choose independently. This structure can be especially useful for learners who struggle to organize their own education.\n\nUniversities can also provide broader knowledge. A software developer, for example, may benefit from studying mathematics, computer architecture, algorithms, communication, and ethics instead of learning only the programming language required for a particular job. Some of these subjects may not produce immediate practical results, but they can help students understand the principles behind technology.\n\nAnother advantage is access to people and opportunities. Universities bring students into contact with teachers, classmates, researchers, clubs, and professional networks. These relationships can lead to internships, projects, recommendations, and future employment. For some students, the network they build during university becomes almost as valuable as the academic knowledge itself.\n\nHowever, university education has limitations. It can be expensive, and the curriculum may change more slowly than the technology industry. A student might spend years studying a subject only to discover that employers are looking for skills that have recently become more important.\n\nSelf-directed learning offers a different model. Someone can identify a skill that companies currently need, study it online, build projects, and apply for jobs without waiting several years to complete a degree. This approach can be faster and more flexible.\n\nYet flexibility can also create problems. Online learners must decide what to study, which resources to trust, how deeply to study each subject, and when they are ready to apply for a job. Without a clear structure, it is easy to move from one course to another without developing strong skills.\n\nEmployers face a similar challenge. A degree is a relatively simple signal. It tells an employer that a person completed a long educational process. It does not prove that the person is an excellent programmer, but it provides some information about persistence, discipline, and academic preparation. On the other hand, a strong portfolio can provide direct evidence of practical ability.\n\nThis is why many technology companies increasingly look at multiple signals. They may consider degrees, certificates, portfolios, technical interviews, internships, previous employment, and personal projects. None of these measurements is perfect. A person with a degree may have weak practical skills, while a self-taught developer may be highly capable but have difficulty proving that ability to employers.\n\nThere is also an important difference between entering technology and progressing within it. A person may get their first job through a portfolio or practical test, but long-term success usually requires continuous learning. Technology changes quickly, so the ability to learn new tools may eventually become more important than the specific tools a person learned at the beginning of their career.\n\nFor this reason, the question may be poorly framed. Instead of asking whether degrees are necessary, it may be more useful to ask what a particular career requires. Some technology roles may place greater value on formal education, especially positions involving research, advanced mathematics, or specialized scientific knowledge. Other roles may focus much more heavily on practical skills and demonstrated results.\n\nThe strongest conclusion is therefore not that university is becoming useless. Rather, its role is changing. A degree can provide structure, knowledge, networks, and opportunities, while alternative education can provide speed, flexibility, and direct practical experience.\n\nIn the future, successful technology professionals may come from many different educational backgrounds. What they are likely to share is not a particular certificate or university name, but the ability to demonstrate useful skills, solve problems, communicate effectively, and continue learning as their Solution to Global Food Shortages?","passage":"As the world's population continues to grow, producing enough food is becoming a major challenge. Traditional agriculture depends heavily on land, water, weather, and transportation. At the same time, cities are expanding, while farmland is becoming more limited in some regions. These pressures have encouraged scientists, engineers, and entrepreneurs to explore unusual ways of growing food. One of the most interesting ideas is vertical farming.\n\nInstead of growing crops across large areas of land, vertical farms produce plants in stacked layers inside buildings. Some farms operate in warehouses, while others use specially designed structures. Because the environment can be controlled, farmers can adjust temperature, humidity, light, and the amount of water plants receive. In theory, this allows crops to grow throughout the year, even in places where traditional farming would be difficult.\n\nOne major advantage of vertical farming is its efficient use of space. A building can produce food on several levels rather than using only the ground. This could be particularly useful near large cities, where land is expensive and transportation from rural farms can take time. If vegetables are grown close to consumers, they may reach supermarkets and restaurants more quickly.\n\nWater use is another area where vertical farming can be efficient. Many systems use hydroponics or similar methods, in which plants grow without traditional soil. Water can circulate through the system and be reused instead of simply disappearing into the ground. This does not mean that vertical farms require no water, but they can potentially use it more carefully than some conventional systems.\n\nThere are also environmental benefits. Indoor farms can reduce the distance food travels from the place where it is produced to the place where it is consumed. This may reduce some transportation needs. In addition, controlled environments can protect plants from certain insects and diseases, which may reduce the need for pesticides.\n\nHowever, vertical farming has a serious weakness: energy consumption. Plants still need light, and indoor farms may require powerful artificial lighting, cooling, heating, and ventilation systems. If the electricity comes mainly from fossil fuels, the environmental advantages can become smaller. A farm that saves water but uses enormous amounts of energy may not be as sustainable as it first appears.\n\nCost is another obstacle. Building and maintaining a high-tech farm requires expensive equipment and skilled workers. Traditional farmers already have land, experience, and established systems. A new vertical farm must compete with these systems while also paying for electricity, technology, buildings, and maintenance.\n\nThere is also a question about what vertical farms should actually grow. Leafy vegetables and herbs are often suitable because they grow relatively quickly and do not require enormous amounts of space. Large crops such as wheat, rice, or corn are much more difficult to produce economically in vertical systems. Since these crops provide a large portion of the world's calories, vertical farming cannot currently replace traditional agriculture completely.\n\nFor this reason, some researchers argue that the most realistic future is not a choice between vertical farming and traditional farming. Instead, the two systems could complement each other. Outdoor agriculture could continue producing crops that require large amounts of space, while vertical farms could specialize in certain vegetables and crops close to urban consumers.\n\nThe location of these farms may also change. In wealthy cities, vertical farming may provide fresh local food and reduce dependence on distant supply chains. In regions with extreme climates, it could offer another advantage by protecting crops from heat, cold, drought, or unpredictable weather.\n\nStill, technology alone cannot solve every food problem. Food shortages are connected to poverty, distribution, political instability, waste, and access to resources. Producing more food does not automatically guarantee that everyone can afford or receive it.\n\nVertical farming should therefore be seen as one possible tool rather than a complete solution. Its success will depend on energy sources, costs, crop choices, and local conditions. The most promising approach may be a combination of technologies and traditional methods rather than a single revolutionary system.\n\nThe idea is exciting because it challenges a basic assumption about agriculture: food does not always have to be grown outdoors, on horizontal fields. But whether vertical farming becomes a major part of the global food system will depend not only on what engineers can build, but also on whether those systems can become affordable, efficient, and feature of professional life. Before the experiment began, managers were concerned that clients might receive slower responses and that employees might struggle to complete their usual workload. Employees, meanwhile, were enthusiastic but uncertain. They expected to have more free time, but some wondered whether the shorter week would simply create more pressure during the remaining four days.\n\nThe company began by examining how employees actually spent their time. Managers discovered that a significant amount of working time was lost to unnecessary meetings, repeated discussions, and interruptions. Some employees also checked email constantly, even when doing tasks that required concentration.\n\nInstead of simply removing Friday from the calendar, the company changed its working habits. Meetings were shortened, some were cancelled, and employees were encouraged to protect periods of uninterrupted work. In some workplaces, long hours are still associated with commitment and ambition. Employees may worry that leaving earlier makes them look less serious. Online: B1 Mastery | Lessons 34–36","passage":"Every day, people encounter thousands of pieces of information online. Some are carefully researched, while others are incomplete, misleading, or completely false. The problem is not simply that false information exists. The bigger challenge is that misleading content can look convincing, especially when it confirms something a person already believes.\n\nMisinformation can take many forms. A social media post may contain a real photograph but provide a false explanation of when or where it was taken. A headline may exaggerate the facts in an article. A video may show a genuine event while using an unrelated description. Sometimes information is not entirely false but is presented without enough context to create a misleading impression.\n\nThe first step in evaluating information is to slow down. Emotional content often spreads quickly because it creates surprise, anger, fear, or excitement. A person who immediately shares a dramatic story may help distribute it before checking whether it is accurate. Taking a few seconds to ask “How do I know this is true?” can prevent many mistakes.\n\nThe source should be examined carefully. Who published the information? Is the organization identifiable? Does the website provide contact information and explain who is responsible for its content? A professional-looking website is not necessarily a reliable one. Design can be copied, logos can be used without permission, and confident language can create a false impression of authority.\n\nThe next step is to look for the original source. If an article claims that a scientist made a particular statement, it is useful to find the original interview, research paper, speech, or official document. Secondary sources can summarize information incorrectly, intentionally or unintentionally. Going back to the original evidence makes it easier to understand what was actually said.\n\nDates are also important. Old photographs and articles are frequently shared as if they describe recent events. A photograph of a flood from several years ago may suddenly appear online with a new location attached to it. The image itself may be genuine, but the claim surrounding it may be false.\n\nImages and videos require special attention. Technology makes it easier to edit visual content, remove context, or combine real material with misleading information. However, people do not always need advanced technical tools to investigate an image. They can search for earlier versions, compare different reports, or examine whether reputable organizations describe the same event.\n\nAnother useful method is comparison. Instead of depending on one post, look for independent sources. If several reliable organizations report the same event and provide similar evidence, confidence increases. If a surprising claim appears on only one unknown website while established sources report nothing similar, caution is appropriate.\n\nIt is also important to recognize confirmation bias. People naturally prefer information that supports their existing opinions. This means a false story can become especially powerful when it tells readers exactly what they want to believe. Being skeptical should therefore apply to information we disagree with and information we strongly agree with.\n\nThe language of a message can provide clues as well. Claims such as “Everyone is hiding this,” “You won't believe what happened,” or “Share this before it gets deleted” are designed to create urgency. Urgency can reduce careful thinking. Reliable information does not become true simply because it is presented dramatically.\n\nHowever, verification has limits. Ordinary users may not have enough time or expertise to investigate every claim completely. The goal is not to become an expert in every subject. Instead, people should learn when to pause, when to question a source, and when not to share something they cannot verify.\n\nCorrecting misinformation also requires care. If someone shares false information, attacking the person may make them defensive. A more effective approach may be to present the evidence calmly and explain how the mistake occurred.\n\nUltimately, media literacy is not about believing nothing. It is about developing a better process for deciding what deserves belief. The internet gives individuals access to an enormous amount of information, but access alone does not guarantee understanding.\n\nThe most reliable online reader is therefore not the person who knows every fact. People buy coffee with a phone, pay for public transport with a card, or transfer money to a friend within seconds. For businesses, digital payments can make transactions faster and easier to record. For customers, they often provide convenience. However, as societies move toward cashless systems, an important question appears: Does greater convenience for most people create new difficulties for others?\n\nOne clear advantage of cashless payments is speed. A customer does not need to count coins or wait for change. Businesses can also reduce the amount of cash they keep on their premises, which may lower certain security risks. Digital transactions create records as well, making it easier for people to check their spending and for businesses to organize their accounts.\n\nDigital payments can also make economic activity more flexible. Some older people may feel uncomfortable using unfamiliar payment applications. A person with limited digital skills may struggle to create an account, remember a password, or solve a technical problem. People with limited access to banking services may face even greater difficulties. If a shop refuses cash, these customers may have no practical way to pay.\n\nThis problem is sometimes described as social exclusion. A system may appear efficient when viewed from the perspective of the majority, while quietly making everyday life harder for a minority. The issue is not necessarily that people refuse to learn new technology. In some cases, they may not have reliable internet access, a suitable device, a bank account, or the financial resources needed to participate fully in the digital economy.\n\nThere are other concerns too. Digital payment systems depend on technology. A power failure, network problem, software error, or cyberattack could temporarily prevent people from paying. Cash does not depend on a mobile network or a functioning payment server. For this reason, some businesses and policymakers argue that keeping cash available can provide an important backup.\n\nPrivacy is another complicated issue. Cash transactions usually reveal little information about the buyer. Digital payments, however, can create detailed records about where, when, and sometimes how people spend their money. Such information can be useful for financial management and fraud detection, but it can also raise questions about who has access to the data and how long it is stored.\n\nThe debate, therefore, is not simply about whether cash is old-fashioned and digital payments are modern. It should also be judged by whether people with different ages, incomes, abilities, and levels of technological experience can participate. When people want to buy a pair of shoes, they may have hundreds of designs available online. When they want to watch a film, streaming platforms can offer thousands of titles. Even simple decisions, such as choosing a restaurant or selecting a phone plan, can require comparing many possibilities.\n\nAt first, having more options seems obviously positive. Choice gives people freedom. It allows them to search for something that fits their preferences instead of accepting whatever is available. However, psychologists and researchers have long been interested in a surprising possibility: more choice can sometimes make people less satisfied rather than more satisfied.\n\nThis idea is often called the paradox of choice. The problem is not that people dislike freedom. Rather, when the number of alternatives becomes too large, choosing can require too much mental effort. Instead of feeling empowered, a person may become uncertain, tired, or anxious.\n\nImagine someone looking for a new laptop. If there are three suitable models, the decision may be relatively simple. But if there are fifty models with different processors, screen sizes, prices, batteries, and features, the buyer may begin comparing tiny differences. After making a decision, the person might continue wondering whether another model would have been better.\n\nThis leads to another psychological problem: regret. When only a few realistic choices exist, people may accept that no option is perfect. When dozens of alternatives are available, however, it becomes easier to imagine that a better choice was possible. The result can be dissatisfaction even when the original decision was perfectly reasonable.\n\nChoice overload is not limited to shopping. It can appear in education, employment, entertainment, and digital platforms. A student may become confused when presented with hundreds of online courses without guidance. A job seeker may spend hours moving between vacancies without applying to any. A person using a streaming service may spend longer choosing what to watch than actually watching something.\n\nThe digital world can make this problem more intense because options are constantly presented to us. Websites recommend products, applications suggest videos, and social media platforms provide an endless stream of content. The user does not simply choose from a list; the list keeps changing.\n\nOne useful response is to establish criteria before making a decision. Instead of asking, “Which laptop is the best?” a buyer could ask, “Which laptop is good enough for my budget, studies, and daily work?” This changes the goal from finding the perfect option to finding an option that satisfies important requirements.\n\nAnother strategy is to limit the number of alternatives. A person might compare only three or four products that meet their basic criteria. This does not remove freedom; it makes freedom easier to use.\n\nDefaults can also reduce unnecessary decision-making. For example, a company might provide a standard software package for employees rather than asking every employee to choose from dozens of possibilities. Individuals can create similar defaults in their personal lives, such as having a regular breakfast, a preferred study schedule, or a small list of trusted websites.\n\nTime boundaries are another useful tool. Some decisions deserve careful research, but others do not. Spending two hours comparing inexpensive headphones may not produce enough additional value to justify the time. Setting a deadline can prevent a small decision from consuming an unreasonable amount of attention.\n\nThis does not mean that fewer choices are always better. For important decisions, having several alternatives can reveal opportunities that would otherwise remain invisible. The real challenge is finding a useful balance between freedom and overload.\n\nThe paradox of choice therefore teaches a broader lesson about modern life. Having more possibilities does not automatically improve our experience. Sometimes the ability to choose well depends on our ability to ignore unnecessary choices. By setting criteria, reducing alternatives, using sensible defaults, and recognizing when a decision is important enough to deserve more time, people can protect their attention without giving up is difficult. New technologies can develop faster than expected, economic conditions can change suddenly, and social habits can move in directions that were difficult to imagine only a few years earlier. Yet instead of asking exactly what the future will look like, it may be more useful to identify the forces that are likely to shape it.\n\nOne of the strongest forces is the continuing development of digital technology and artificial intelligence. AI tools are already changing how people search for information, create content, analyze data, and complete technical tasks. The important question is not simply whether machines will replace workers. In many fields, the more realistic possibility is that the tasks people perform will change. Workers may spend less time on repetitive activities and more time checking results, solving unusual problems, communicating with others, and making decisions.\n\nThis shift could also change education. If information becomes easier to access, memorizing facts may become less important than knowing how to evaluate information and use it effectively. However, access to technology does not automatically produce learning. Students still need discipline, guidance, communication skills, and the ability to recognize unreliable information. The future of education may therefore involve a combination of technology and human support rather than a simple replacement of teachers by software.\n\nWork itself may become more flexible. Remote and hybrid employment have already shown that some jobs can be performed from different locations. At the same time, flexibility can create new challenges. Employees may need stronger communication habits, better time management, and greater awareness of cybersecurity. Companies may also need to rethink how they measure productivity. Being online for many hours is not necessarily the same as producing valuable work.\n\nCities will face another set of pressures. Smart systems can improve transportation, manage energy use, and help public services respond to problems. Yet the collection of large amounts of data raises questions about privacy and surveillance. A city that knows more about its residents may operate more efficiently, but efficiency without transparency can damage public trust.\n\nEnvironmental pressure will also influence decisions. Renewable energy, electric transport, improved farming methods, and more efficient buildings may reduce some environmental problems. However, no single technology can solve climate and food challenges by itself. Energy systems require infrastructure, new technologies require resources, and agricultural problems involve not only production but also poverty, distribution, waste, and access.\n\nHealth care may become more connected to technology as well. Telemedicine can make medical advice easier to access, especially for people who live far from specialists. At the same time, some medical situations still require physical examination or direct observation. The most effective systems may therefore combine digital services with traditional medical care rather than choosing one and rejecting the other.\n\nAnother major challenge will be the information environment. People now have access to an enormous amount of news, commentary, advertising, and user-generated content. This creates opportunities for education and communication, but it also makes misinformation easier to spread. A person who wants to make good decisions will need more than access to information. They will need the ability to question sources, compare evidence, recognize emotional manipulation, and admit uncertainty.\n\nGlobalization will continue to connect people, businesses, and cultures, but it will not eliminate differences between them. Migration, international work, online communities, and global markets can expose people to new ideas and opportunities. At the same time, cultural identity remains important. Food, language, traditions, and local communities can help people maintain a sense of belonging while adapting to new environments.\n\nAcross all these areas, one pattern becomes visible: adaptation may become more important than prediction. It is impossible for an individual, company, or government to know exactly which technologies will succeed or which problems will become most urgent. What they can do is build the ability to learn, adjust, evaluate evidence, and respond responsibly.\n\nThe next decade, therefore, is unlikely to be shaped by one invention alone. It will be shaped by the interaction between technology, economics, education, work, health, the environment, information, and human behavior. The people and organizations that succeed may not necessarily be those that predict the future perfectly.                 let s=String(v??"").trim().toLowerCase().replace(/[’‘]/g,"'");
                const contractions={"doesn't":"does not","don't":"do not","didn't":"did not","isn't":"is not","aren't":"are not","wasn't":"was not","weren't":"were not","can't":"cannot","couldn't":"could not","won't":"will not","wouldn't":"would not","shouldn't":"should not","mustn't":"must not","haven't":"have not","hasn't":"has not","hadn't":"had not"};
                Object.keys(contractions).forEach(k=>{s=s.replace(new RegExp('\\b'+k.replace(/[.*+?^${}()|[\]\\]/g,'\\$&')+'\\b','g'),contractions[k]);});
                return s.replace(/[^a-z0-9]+/g," ").replace(/\s+/g," ").trim();
            };
            /* ===== Writing AI configuration ===== */
            // Security: never ship a private API key inside the browser bundle.
            // Production should expose a server-side proxy through window.GROQ_WRITING_ENDPOINT.
            const GROQ_API_KEY = window.GROQ_API_KEY || "";
            const GROQ_ENDPOINT = window.GROQ_WRITING_ENDPOINT || "https://api.groq.com/openai/v1/chat/completions";
            const GROQ_MODEL = window.GROQ_WRITING_MODEL || "openai/gpt-oss-120b";

            const parseGroqJson=(content)=>{
                if(typeof content!=="string") return content||{};
                let clean=content.trim();
                clean=clean.replace(/^```json\s*/i,"").replace(/^```\s*/i,"").replace(/\s*```$/i,"").trim();
                try{return JSON.parse(clean);}catch(e){
                    const first=clean.indexOf("{");
                    const last=clean.lastIndexOf("}");
                    if(first>=0&&last>first){
                        try{return JSON.parse(clean.slice(first,last+1));}catch(_){}}
                }
                throw new Error("Groq returned an invalid JSON response.");
            };

            const checkWritingWithGroq=async(text)=>{
                const systemPrompt=`You are the B1 English writing evaluator inside an educational platform.
Analyze the learner's English paragraph carefully. Evaluate it against the task instructions and B1 expectations. Do NOT rewrite the whole paragraph automatically.
Return ONLY valid JSON with exactly these fields:
{
  "overallScore": number,
  "grammarScore": number,
  "spellingScore": number,
  "punctuationScore": number,
  "naturalnessScore": number,
  "wordCount": number,
  "summary": string,
  "correctedParagraph": string,
  "errors": [
    {
      "text": string,
      "type": string,
      "message": string,
      "correction": string,
      "explanation": string
    }
  ],
  "strengths": [string],
  "improvements": [string]
}
Rules:
- Score each score from 0 to 100.
- wordCount must count the learner's words.
- Find real grammar, spelling, punctuation, word-choice, and unnatural-English issues.
- Keep correctedParagraph faithful to the learner's meaning; it may be fully corrected but must not invent new information.
- Explain errors simply for an English learner.
- If there are no errors, errors must be [].
- Do not require C1/C2 complexity; however, the response should meet B1 expectations for grammar, vocabulary, cohesion, and task achievement.
- The task is a daily-routine paragraph using Present Simple.`;
                const userPrompt=`Learner paragraph:\n\n${text}`;
                const controller=new AbortController();
                const timer=setTimeout(()=>controller.abort(),30000);
                try{
                    const res=await fetch(GROQ_ENDPOINT,{
                        method:"POST",
                        headers:{
                            "Content-Type":"application/json",
                            "Authorization":`Bearer ${GROQ_API_KEY}`
                        },
                        body:JSON.stringify({
                            model:GROQ_MODEL,
                            temperature:0,
                            response_format:{type:"json_object"},
                            reasoning_effort:"low",
                            messages:[
                                {role:"system",content:systemPrompt},
                                {role:"user",content:userPrompt}
                            ]
                        }),
                        signal:controller.signal,
                        cache:"no-store"
                    });
                    const raw=await res.text();
                    if(!res.ok){
                        let detail=raw;
                        try{const j=JSON.parse(raw);detail=j.error?.message||detail;}catch(_){ }
                        throw new Error(`Groq HTTP ${res.status}: ${detail}`);
                    }
                    const data=JSON.parse(raw);
                    const content=data?.choices?.[0]?.message?.content;
                    if(!content) throw new Error("لم تصل نتيجة من Groq.");
                    return parseGroqJson(content);
                }finally{
                    clearTimeout(timer);
                }

            const renderWriting=()=>{

                    id:q.id,
                    title:`السؤال ${q.number} — ${q.type}`,

                    answer:q.answer,
                    openEnded:false
                }));
                const allQuestionsAnswered=questions.every(q=>String(writingAnswers[q.id]||"").trim()!=="");
                const runAllWritingQuestions=()=>{
                    if(!allQuestionsAnswered){
                        setWritingExerciseFeedback(<div className="notice-box">⚠️ أكمل جميع أسئلة الكتابة أولًا.</div>);
                        return;
                    }
                    const results=questions.map(q=>{
                        const answer=String(writingAnswers[q.id]||"").trim();
                        const wordsInAnswer=answer.split(/\s+/).filter(Boolean);
                        const englishOnly=!containsArabic(answer);
                        let ok=englishOnly && wordsInAnswer.length>=2;
                        let message="";
                        if(!englishOnly){
                            ok=false;
                            message="اكتب الإجابة باللغة الإنجليزية فقط.";
                        }else if(wordsInAnswer.length<2){
                            ok=false;
                            message="اكتب إجابة كاملة من كلمتين على الأقل.";
                        }else if(q.openEnded){
                            ok=true;
                            message="تم قبول المهمة القصيرة. الفقرة النهائية لها فحص مستقل بواسطة أداة التصحيح.";
                        }else{
                            const normalized=normalizeExerciseAnswer(answer);
                            const expected=normalizeExerciseAnswer(q.answer);
                            const aTokens=normalized.split(/\s+/).filter(Boolean);
                            const eTokens=expected.split(/\s+/).filter(Boolean);
                            const common=eTokens.filter(t=>aTokens.includes(t)).length;
                            const coverage=eTokens.length ? common/eTokens.length : 0;
                            const editDistance=(a,b)=>{
                                const dp=Array.from({length:a.length+1},()=>Array(b.length+1).fill(0));
                                for(let i=0;i<=a.length;i++) dp[i][0]=i;
                                for(let j=0;j<=b.length;j++) dp[0][j]=j;
                                for(let i=1;i<=a.length;i++) for(let j=1;j<=b.length;j++)
                                    dp[i][j]=a[i-1]===b[j-1]?dp[i-1][j-1]:Math.min(dp[i-1][j]+1,dp[i][j-1]+1,dp[i-1][j-1]+1);
                                return dp[a.length][b.length];
                            };
                            const similarity=expected.length ? 1-(editDistance(normalized,expected)/Math.max(normalized.length,expected.length,1)) : 0;
                            // Controlled tasks accept the model answer or a very close equivalent variant.
                            ok=normalized===expected || similarity>=0.86 || (coverage>=0.90 && Math.abs(aTokens.length-eTokens.length)<=3);
                            message=ok ? "✓ إجابة مقبولة. تمت مقارنة إجابتك بالمطلوب مع السماح بصياغات بديلة قريبة." : "الإجابة تحتاج مراجعة. تأكد من القاعدة المطلوبة وترتيب الكلمات والمعنى ثم أعد المحاولة.";
                        }
                        return {id:q.id,ok,matches:[],corrected:answer,message};
                    });
                    const ok=results.every(r=>r.ok);
                    setWritingResults(results);
                    setWritingExerciseSolved(ok);

className="main-workspace full-width skill-home"><div className="home-head"><div><span style={{color:"var(--primary)",fontWeight:800}}>{s.icon} {s.title}</span><h1>{activeLesson?activeLesson.title:"مرحبًا بك في قسم "+s.title}</h1><p>{activeLesson?"أكمل الدرس بالكامل لفتح الدرس التالي.":s.desc}</p></div><div style={{minWidth:220}}><b>تقدم القسم: {progressFor(activeSkill)}%</b><ProgressBar value={progressFor(activeSkill)}/></div></div><div className="skill-shell"><section className="lesson-panel">{activeLesson?renderLesson():renderSectionHome()}</section><aside className="lesson-sidebar"><h3>📚 فهرس {s.title}</h3>{(indexUnits[activeSkill]||[]).map((unit,ui)=>{const unitKey=`${activeSkill}-u${ui}`;const isOpen=!!openUnits[unitKey];let start=0;for(let k=0;k<ui;k++)start+=(indexUnits[activeSkill][k]?.[1]?.length||0);return <div className="accordion-item" key={unitKey}><button type="button" className="accordion-btn" onClick={()=>setOpenUnits(p=>({...p,[unitKey]:!p[unitKey]}))}><span>{unit[0]}</span><span>{isOpen?"▾":"▸"}</span></button>{isOpen&&<div className="sub-lessons-wrapper">{unit[1].map((title,li)=>{const actual=skillLessons[activeSkill]?.[start+li];const done=actual?!!completed[actual.id]:false;const unlocked=actual?isUnlocked(actual):false;const active=actual&&activeLesson?.id===actual.id;return <button type="button" key={`${unitKey}-l${li}`} disabled={!actual||!unlocked} className={`sub-lesson-btn ${active?"active":""} ${done?"done":""} ${(!actual||!unlocked)?"locked":""}`} onClick={()=>actual&&openLesson(actual)}><span><span className="skill-lesson-number">{done?"✓":(!actual||!unlocked?"🔒":start+li+1)}</span>{title}<span style={{fontSize:"0.68rem",color:"var(--text-muted)",marginRight:"8px",whiteSpace:"nowrap"}}>10 تدريبات</span></span></button>})}</div>}</div>})}<div className="study-box" style={{padding:12,marginTop:14}}><div className="counter">الإنجاز الفعلي</div><ProgressBar value={progressFor(activeSkill)}/></div></aside></div></main></div>;
        }

        ReactDOM.createRoot(document.getElementById('root')).render(<App />);
    </script>
